summary: Sands Point Light, on the North Shore of Long Island, was first shown in 1809, moved offshore to a steel tower in 1922, and has been in private hands since its 1924 sale.

lens.where: not stated; LighthouseFriends says a fifth-order lens was installed in 1856

structures.type: octagonal coursed brownstone tower with cast-iron stairs
structures.note: Remodeled 1868-69 (Bulletin 1924); tower and dwelling connected by a passageway

structures.type: automated steel skeleton tower on a reef offshore
structures.note: Light moved here on 15 December 1922, about 800 feet offshore from the old light

access.note: Privately owned; not open to the public. The only view for visitors is from the water.

events.note: Act of Congress for a light at Sands Point, 26 January 1806
About five acres bought from Benjamin Hewlett; sources date the purchase 1808 (July for the United States; January 15 for the state; 1808 for New York)
Brownstone tower completed by November 1809 by Noah Mason and Way of New London
Light first shown 9 September 1809
LighthouseFriends: fifth-order Fresnel lens. The 1895 Light-House Board report and the USLHS record describe a fourth-order light
New lantern room placed atop the tower
Congress allocated $9,400 to renovate the tower and replace the keeper's house
Tower rebuilt and dwelling reconstructed in brick, joined to the tower by a passageway (1868-69)
Changed from a flashing white light every thirty seconds to fixed white, 31 May 1892
Discontinued 31 October 1894 as no longer needed
Reestablished 21 January 1895 at the request of mariners
LighthouseFriends says keeper Cornelius Douglass was recognized for assistance to a woman shot on the beach; not corroborated in the Bulletin or the newspapers checked
Thomas J. Murray transferred from Esopus Meadows to take charge of Sands Point
Wealthy New York socialite bought land beside the lighthouse and built a mansion there
Light moved to an automated steel skeleton tower about 800 feet offshore on a reef, 15 December 1922
Unwatched acetylene light on a skeleton tower on a concrete foundation (Bulletin)
Old light discontinued (USLHS Year Discontinued 1922)
Sale of the station on 31 January 1924 for $100,000 (Bulletin). LighthouseFriends dates the Belmont purchase to 31 January 1923
Mansion and lighthouse sold to William Randolph Hearst for $400,000
Hearsts surrendered the property to a New York bank to satisfy a mortgage
Designated a village landmark by the Village of Sands Point
Rededication after extensive renovations (23 October 2015)

corrections.why: The 1806 date is the act of Congress (26 January 1806). Construction began in 1808 and the tower was complete by November 1809 (Cow Neck society). The USLHS place record gives 1809 as the year established.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The old light was discontinued in December 1922 when the light moved offshore (USLHS Year Discontinued 1922; Cow Neck society and LighthouseFriends give December 1922). The record's 1922 date stands.

LighthouseFriends dates Mrs. O. H. P. Belmont's purchase to 31 January 1923. The Lighthouse Service Bulletin of 1 April 1924 dates the sale to 31 January 1924, and the Bulletin is the official account, so the story follows it and notes the difference.
The roster gives Cornelius Douglass 1895-1916 and Thomas J. Murray 1917-1922. LighthouseFriends prose gives Douglass's tenure ending in 1917, while its own keeper list gives 1916. The roster is used.

notes_for_editor: (1) Tower height: 40 ft (LighthouseFriends), about 50 ft and 65 ft above water (Cow Neck society), 64.5 ft above high water (USLHS). The record's 20.0 m is not settled; focal_height_m 19.7 is the USLHS figure. (2) Lens order: LighthouseFriends says fifth-order in 1856; the 1895 Light-House Board report calls the light fourth-order; the USLHS record lists a fourth-order Fresnel. Not reconciled. (3) Birth year of Noah Mason: 1757 (Cow Neck society, quoting pension papers) vs 1755 (LighthouseFriends). (4) Contract and cost: appropriation $6,000 (LighthouseFriends), low bid $8,500 by Mason (Keeper's Log 1989), contract to Mason and Way (Cow Neck). The Keeper's Log OCR garbles some dates (1806, 1809); only the bid sentence is quoted. (5) Land purchase: 1806 (state act, Cow Neck), 15 Jan 1808 (state purchase, via 1927 article quoted by Cow Neck), 1808 (New York for $512.50, LighthouseFriends), July 1808 (United States, Bulletin). Not reconciled. (6) Douglass tenure: roster 1895-1916; LighthouseFriends prose 1917. Roster used. (7) Seaman: LighthouseFriends says he remained until death in 1895; roster shows 1866-1894 and a Jan-July 1895 stint. Both are given. (8) The 1913 shooting-assistance item rests on LighthouseFriends alone; a newspaper search for 1912-1917 (New-York Tribune, Sun) did not show it within the search budget. (9) The Belmont date: LighthouseFriends 31 Jan 1923; Bulletin 31 Jan 1924 (Bulletin used). Wikipedia gives February 1924; not used. (10) Mason's 1814/1813 gunboat battle dates conflict: LighthouseFriends 10 Sept 1814; Mitchill's memoir as printed by the Cow Neck society, September 1813. Both are stated. (11) Not used: longislandlighthouses.com (its domain now carries unrelated spam content); Port Washington Library PDF (cdm16694, fetch returned nothing); HAER NY-93 (loc.gov, not called directly per the guide). (12) Wikipedia is lead-only and not cited. (13) Page-read budget: roughly 10 web reads and the corpus, within the guide's 15. (14) Fact-check pass, 2026-10-28: the 1927 source is a newspaper article by William M. Hyde, quoted by the Cow Neck society, and is now described as such. The Bache 1838 figure is LighthouseFriends' report, not a quotation, and is now attributed that way. The lens order disagreement (fifth order in LighthouseFriends; fourth order in the 1895 report and the USLHS record) is now stated in the story. The 1868-69 remodel is cited to the 1924 Bulletin page 16, checked against the cached PDF text. The Keeper's Log 1989 bid and the 1895 report quotations were checked against their sources. The page images were not opened.
